name: Job Syndrome (Autosomal Dominant Hyper-IgE Syndrome, STAT3 Deficiency)

clinicalPearls: Classic triad is recurrent staphylococcal skin and lung abscesses, chronic eczematoid dermatitis, and markedly elevated serum IgE.
Caused by dominant-negative mutations in STAT3, impairing Th17 differentiation and thereby mucocutaneous defence against Staphylococcus aureus and Candida.
Pulmonary abscesses and pneumonias heal with pneumatoceles and bronchiectasis, which later become niches for Aspergillus and Pseudomonas superinfection.
Skin abscesses are characteristically 'cold', lacking the usual warmth, erythema and systemic signs of inflammation.

A distinctive multisystem, non-immune phenotype includes a coarse facial appearance, retained primary teeth, hyperextensible joints, scoliosis, osteopenia with minimal-trauma fractures, and arterial aneurysms.
Blood eosinophilia is common; the very high IgE may fall towards normal in adulthood and does not correlate with disease severity.
A clinical scoring system combining immunological and connective-tissue features aids recognition, with STAT3 sequencing confirming the diagnosis.
Management relies on long-term anti-staphylococcal and antifungal prophylaxis, aggressive treatment of infections and skin care rather than routine immunoglobulin replacement.
reference.pathophysiology: Job syndrome is caused by heterozygous dominant-negative mutations in STAT3, a transcription factor that transduces signals from numerous cytokine receptors including IL-6, IL-10, IL-21 and IL-23. Because the mutant protein interferes with the normal allele, STAT3-dependent signalling is broadly impaired. A pivotal consequence is failure of Th17 cell differentiation, since STAT3 is required downstream of IL-6 and IL-23 for RORgammaT-driven Th17 commitment; the resulting deficiency of IL-17 and IL-22 cripples the recruitment of neutrophils and the induction of epithelial antimicrobial peptides at skin and mucosal surfaces, explaining the striking susceptibility to Staphylococcus aureus and mucocutaneous Candida. Impaired STAT3 signalling also disturbs class-switching and the germinal-centre response, producing dysregulated, grossly elevated IgE and diminished memory B-cell generation, and blunts the acute-phase and inflammatory responses so that infections are paradoxically 'cold'. Beyond immunity, STAT3 participates in tissue remodelling, bone metabolism and vascular integrity, so its loss produces the characteristic skeletal, dental, facial and connective-tissue abnormalities and predisposes to aneurysm formation, making the disorder a true multisystem syndrome rather than a pure immunodeficiency.
additionalDifferentials: Autosomal recessive hyper-IgE syndromes (for example DOCK8 deficiency)
Severe atopic dermatitis with recurrent infection
Netherton syndrome and other ichthyosiform disorders with high IgE
Omenn syndrome and other combined immunodeficiencies
additionalInvestigations: Serum IgE with serial monitoring and full blood count for eosinophilia
STAT3 gene sequencing to confirm the diagnosis
Th17 (IL-17-producing CD4) cell enumeration by flow cytometry
High-resolution chest imaging for pneumatoceles and bronchiectasis
Skeletal survey or bone density assessment for fractures and osteopenia
Vascular imaging to screen for coronary and other arterial aneurysms
Microbiological and fungal cultures of sputum and abscess material
redFlags: Haemoptysis or cavitary lung lesions suggesting Aspergillus or Pseudomonas superinfection of pneumatoceles
Rapidly enlarging or ruptured arterial aneurysm
Recurrent minimal-trauma fractures indicating significant osteopenia
Systemic candidiasis or invasive fungal disease
A 'cold' abscess with few systemic signs masking severe underlying infection
reference.prognosis: With sustained antimicrobial prophylaxis and vigilant management of pulmonary and skin infection, many patients reach adulthood, though chronic lung damage, invasive fungal infection and vascular complications remain important causes of morbidity and premature death.
pitfalls: Relying on the absolute IgE level, which fluctuates and may normalise in adults, to include or exclude the diagnosis
Missing serious infection because abscesses are 'cold' and lack expected inflammatory signs
Overlooking the connective-tissue, skeletal and vascular features and treating it as isolated severe eczema
Failing to distinguish it from DOCK8 and other autosomal recessive hyper-IgE syndromes, which differ in viral susceptibility and prognosis
Neglecting to protect and monitor pneumatoceles that later seed fungal superinfection
management: Give continuous antistaphylococcal antibiotic prophylaxis (such as cotrimoxazole) to curb recurrent staphylococcal skin and pulmonary abscesses
Provide antifungal prophylaxis against mucocutaneous Candida and Aspergillus superinfection of pneumatoceles
Control the eczematoid dermatitis with emollients, topical anti-inflammatories and antiseptic bleach baths
Treat established infections with prompt culture-guided antimicrobials and drainage of abscesses
Perform serial high-resolution chest imaging surveillance for pneumatoceles and bronchiectasis and act early on fungal colonisation
Monitor the skeleton and dentition for osteopenia, fractures, scoliosis and retained primary teeth, and screen arteries for aneurysm
Consider immunoglobulin replacement or haematopoietic stem cell transplantation in selected severe cases
Offer autosomal dominant genetic counselling and family assessment
